name: Supporting First Generation Families
title: Supporting First Generation Families
answer: Supporting first generation families means giving students whose parents did not attend college and their families clear help with applications, financial aid, and campus life. The book argues this targeted support is worth the investment because these families may not know how the process works. It also warns that family support should be designed carefully, since one trial found that adding parents to text messages did not increase the effect.

sections.body: First generation students face extra hurdles because their parents may not have experience with college applications, financial aid, or campus life. The problem is not that families do not care, but that the process can be unfamiliar and hard to navigate without guidance. The book says the chatbot trial found that first generation students gained the most from outreach during the summer. It concludes that targeted support for these students and families is worth the investment. At the same time, it notes that schools should think carefully about what kind of family support actually helps.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Schools can help first generation families understand the college process through family nights, translated guides, and personal conversations. TalkingPoints can carry messages in families' languages, as Chapter 14 described. BigFuture offers information families can explore together. The goal is for families to feel confident supporting their children, not overwhelmed. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so these practices are described for schools and families generally.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites two trials. The chatbot trial found that first generation students gained the most from outreach during the summer (Nurshatayeva et al., 2021). In another trial, adding parents to text messages did not increase the effect (Castleman & Page, 2017). Text outreach raised on time enrollment by about 3 points, but messages to parents added nothing beyond messages to students. The book does not attach a formal evidence label to this idea, and it uses these findings to argue for careful design rather than assuming any family contact will help.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The book warns that adding parents to text messages did not increase the effect in one trial, so schools should not assume that more family contact is always better. This does not mean families do not matter. It means schools should think carefully about what kind of family support actually helps. The text does not say that a chatbot or text messages should decide which family supports to use. The aim is to help families feel confident rather than overwhelmed.
